newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian sugar in deep oversupply, trade depressed.
newsitem.headline: Russian sugar in deep oversupply, trade depressed.

text.p: Russia is so awash in refined white sugar that the Agriculture Ministry is using it instead of cash to settle accounts, and traders on Monday saw few prospects of domestic prices recovering before March.
Traders also said oversupply could force Moscow to delay hammering out its next barter deal of Russian oil for Cuban raws in 1997.
"There's not enough demand and prices are very low," said a top trader at a big Western commodities house.
"Nobody really knows how much surplus there is, but my guess is around one million tonnes in various warehouses."
Traders said Menatep-Impex, one of the Russian partners in the most recent oil-for-sugar barter deal, had large, unsold stocks. Menatep could not be reached for comment.
"If they put it out on the market after the New Year, it could really destabilise it," one source said.

While both Russia and big beet producer Ukraine have had poor harvests this year, Russian farmers have depressed prices by turning out in droves to sell what little refined sugar they have produced from their crops.
The kolkhoz sugar, as traders call it, referring to the collective farms where farmers grow beets and then race to refine them for quick cash, has come at a bad time.
"There's a lot of stuff out there," said one source, saying prices were as low as 2000 roubles per kg (equivalent to some $363 per tonne and below the average $460 per tonne wholesale).
"There's so much sugar that the Agriculture Ministry is even using it to pay some of its organisations."
He said the oversupply would last at least until March.
Interfax news agency said Russian refineries -- vocal about their dislike of cheap Ukrainian imports -- were working at an average 55 percent of capacity due to the whites surplus.
But in a change of emphasis, traders are blaming Russia's oversupplied market less on Ukrainian imports and more on big purchases of Cuban raws made earlier in the year.
"Ukraine has more or less stopped dumping," said the second trader. "The oversupply is mostly due to high imports of raws."
He said Ukrainian imports were down 30 percent on peak levels seen before Moscow slapped a 10 percent duty on them in a bid to curb what it called dumping and boost its own refiners.
"It's very tough, but I think that with the bad harvests, things are bound to change," one trader said.
But he said raws buying would not take place until the end of March at the earliest.
Russia's sugar beet harvest is a low 16.0 million tonnes compared to the average over 1991-1995 of 21.7 million tonnes.
Ukraine's beet crop this year is near a low 23.9 million tonnes, from which it will produce around 2.8 million tonnes of refined sugar. It will also refine 561,000 tonnes from imported raws.

Traders said a government plan to slap a $180 tax on all trucks entering Russia was not a talking point. "It's not important when you compare it with the 25 percent import tariff and 10 percent value-added tax," said one of the sources.

Russia -- where yearly white sugar demand is around five million tonnes -- is considering an annual import quota of 1.5 million tonnes of whites, including 1.1 million from Ukraine. --Lynnley Browning, Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
